knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 5.1.3
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly describes the inputs and output object for a simple posterior calculation?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Posterior is the updated distribution. Point estimators under loss and intervals are subsequent summaries, not automatic byproducts of writing posterior.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Prior plus likelihood give posterior distribution. Loss-based point estimate is a further step.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Treating posterior as automatically delivering loss-based point estimator.

choices.label: Prior and likelihood together yield a posterior distribution for the parameter. A loss-based point estimator is a further step summarising that posterior under a chosen loss function.
Having the posterior distribution automatically finishes choosing the Bayesian point estimator under squared-error loss; no further step exists.
Simple posterior means the prior alone; likelihood enters only in frequentist confidence intervals.
The output object is always a credible interval; a full posterior distribution is unnecessary once data are observed.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 5.1.3
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Binomial n=10 with x=3 successes and Beta(2,2) prior. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: State posterior parameters; refuse slogan-Bayes and loss-as-automatic.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Conjugate update gives Beta(5,9). Slogan-Bayes and automatic loss estimators are refusals from the checkpoint stem.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Posterior Beta(5,9). Refuse slogan-Bayes; loss estimator is a further step.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Slogan-Bayes without a posterior or treating posterior as automatic point estimator.

choices.label: Posterior Beta(2+3, 2+7) = Beta(5,9). Bayesian work requires an actual posterior distribution, not a slogan. The posterior is the full distribution; a loss-based point estimator under squared-error loss is a further step.
Bayesian means I believe in Bayes; no posterior distribution is required once the prior is named Beta(2,2).
Posterior Beta(2,2) because the prior dominates with n=10 small; successes add nothing to the parameters.
Having Beta(5,9) finishes choosing the Bayesian point estimator under squared-error loss without further calculation.

worked_example.title: Posterior for Poisson rate with Gamma prior
worked_example.problem_statement: Annual flood claim counts are modelled as Poisson(λ). The prior is Gamma(α, β) with shape-rate parameterisation π(λ) ∝ λ^{α−1} e^{−βλ}, here α = 2, β = 3. A sample of n = 4 independent years has total counts Σyᵢ = 10. State the posterior distribution and its mean.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Add Σyᵢ to the shape and n to the rate before forming the posterior mean.

steps.label: Identify the conjugate update
steps.explanation: For Poisson observations with a Gamma(α, β) shape-rate prior, the posterior is Gamma(α+Σy, β+n).

steps.label: Posterior mean
steps.explanation: Under the shape-rate parameterisation the Gamma mean is shape/rate.

steps.label: Refuse wrong update direction
steps.attempt_cue: State why n enters the rate, not the shape alone.
steps.explanation: Each observation year contributes one unit of exposure to the rate parameter; claim counts update the shape.
steps.calculation: Shape += total counts; rate += number of years
steps.result: Do not add n to the shape and Σy to the rate

worked_example.final_answer: Posterior is Gamma(12, 7) with mean 12/7 ≈ 1.7143 claims per year.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Swapping the updates (adding n to the shape and Σy to the rate), or treating the Gamma as shape-scale when the brief specifies shape-rate.
